Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus sits with his hands folded in his lap, his posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At twenty-two, he has the appearance of someone older—there's a wariness in his eyes that doesn't match his age. He works as an auditor for a mid-sized accounting firm, a position he secured after graduating with honors. His colleagues describe him as meticulous and reliable, though they've noticed he's become increasingly withdrawn over the past eight months.

The trauma occurred last December during his first year in the auditing role. Marcus had stayed late at the office to complete a financial reconciliation—something he did regularly, taking pride in his thoroughness. Around 9 PM, a maintenance worker he'd seen dozens of times in the building approached him in the empty hallway. What followed was a violent assault that Marcus still struggles to speak about directly. The man forced him into a storage closet, and Marcus experienced what he describes only as "the worst thing that's ever happened to me."

He reported it to police, but the investigation stalled. The building's security footage had a gap. Witnesses were inconsistent. The case remains open but inactive. Marcus returned to work after two weeks, believing he could simply move forward. His family, deeply private, encouraged him not to dwell on it. He tried to honor that wish.

But moving forward proved impossible. Within weeks, Marcus noticed he couldn't remain at the office past 5 PM without his heart racing uncontrollably. The hallway where it happened has become impassable—he now takes a longer route through the building, which his coworkers find odd. When his supervisor asked why he was leaving projects incomplete, Marcus couldn't explain the panic that grips him when the office empties out.

Sleep has become fragmented. He lies awake most nights, his mind replaying moments he desperately wants to forget. When he does sleep, he wakes gasping, sometimes finding himself on the floor beside his bed with no memory of getting there. Mornings are the worst. He showers immediately upon waking, sometimes twice, scrubbing until his skin reddens. The feeling of being unclean persists regardless.

At work, he's hypervigilant in ways he doesn't fully recognize. He positions himself facing doorways in meetings. He's startled by unexpected sounds—a colleague dropping a pen sends him into a state of heightened alert that takes minutes to settle. His productivity has declined noticeably. The detailed work that once came naturally now requires enormous concentration, and his mind frequently drifts to worst-case scenarios.

Socially, Marcus has become isolated. He declines invitations from coworkers. His few close friends have largely stopped reaching out after repeated cancellations. He tells himself he's simply busy, but the truth is more complicated—being around others feels exposing, as though people can see what happened to him written across his face. He feels fundamentally changed, separated from his peers by an invisible barrier.

Lately, he's begun having intrusive thoughts about the assault at random moments—while reviewing spreadsheets, while waiting for coffee, while sitting in traffic. These thoughts arrive unbidden and feel overwhelmingly real, as though he's back in that storage closet. He's started avoiding situations that might trigger these memories: he no longer works late, he rarely goes to the office gym, and he's requested a transfer to a different floor.

Marcus knows something is wrong. He recognizes that his life has contracted significantly, that he's no longer the person he was before December. But naming it, addressing it directly, feels impossible. He carries his trauma silently, performing normalcy at work while his internal world remains fractured and unsafe.
